source: Lieder & Griffiths (2020) Resource-rational analysis: understanding human cognition as the optimal use of limited computational resources (BBS 43:e1)
finding: Defines the resource-rational mind as the bounded-optimal program: the best mind a brain can run, scored by expected utility over a lifetime. For one decision, the best heuristic h maximises expected utility of the result minus the expected opportunity cost of the time and resources the heuristic uses (Equations 2 and 3). Eq. 3 is a problem solved by evolution and learning, not by the person on the spot.
numbers: Eq.2: m* = argmax over feasible minds of E[u(life history)]. Eq.3: h* = argmax_h E[u(result)] - E[cost(t_h, resources, opportunity cost per unit time)]. Constraints named: limited elementary operations, limited speed, limited working memory.
quote: people never have to directly solve the constrained optimization problem
limits: A method, not a finished theory. The authors say it is a 'methodological device', and at worst a 'convenient template for slightly less unrealistic as-if explanations'.
agent_relevance: This is the exact rule an S0 gate would approximate: pick the procedure with the best expected result minus compute cost. Our agent can only use it as a design target; the rule itself is not computable per problem.

source: Lieder & Griffiths (2020) Resource-rational analysis: understanding human cognition as the optimal use of limited computational resources (BBS 43:e1) - five-step method (Box 2)
finding: The paradigm has five steps: (1) state the function as a computational-level problem; (2) posit an algorithm class, its costs and the utility of accuracy; (3) find the algorithm that best trades accuracy for cost; (4) test its predictions on data; (5) refine the assumptions and repeat. Stopping is allowed when constraints were modelled reasonably, even if people deviate.
numbers: 5 steps. Named relatives: computational rationality (Lewis et al. 2014), bounded optimality (Russell & Subramanian), rational process models, Gabaix myopic cost-benefit, Sims rational inattention.
limits: Step 5 is 'a double-edged sword': free revision of cost assumptions can overfit idiosyncratic or truly irrational behaviour. Advice: take constraints from independent measures, and judge a model by prediction of phenomena it was not built for.
agent_relevance: Gives a repeatable recipe for deriving a gate rule from a cost model. The warning about refitting costs applies to us: tune gate costs on one benchmark and test on another.

source: Lieder & Griffiths (2020) Resource-rational analysis: understanding human cognition as the optimal use of limited computational resources (BBS 43:e1) - bounded information and adaptation (Eq. 4)
finding: Because the world is not fully known, the heuristic is chosen to be best on average over environments consistent with what the agent has learned (Eq. 4). Adaptation is itself bounded, so people may use 'heuristics for choosing heuristics'. A full theory needs a bounded-optimal learning mechanism for becoming resource-rational.
numbers: Eq.4: h* = argmax_h E_{E|i}[ E[u(result)] - E[cost] ], i = information obtained by experience and evolution.
limits: Applies when adaptation had enough pressure and enough experience. Mechanisms that perform almost equally well give no pressure, so the outcome need not be resource-rational.
agent_relevance: Supports a gate that learns per-problem-class pass rates from our own runs (the schema already says S0 rests on our data) instead of a fixed rule.

source: Lieder & Griffiths (2020) Resource-rational analysis: understanding human cognition as the optimal use of limited computational resources (BBS 43:e1) - probability matching and few samples (review of Vul et al. 2014)
finding: The review says a bounded agent should decide from a single mental sample when executing an action takes at most about three times as long as drawing a sample. That is equal to probability matching. Higher stakes raise the best number of samples, and choice moves from matching toward maximising as incentives rise.
numbers: Stated threshold: 'at most three times as long'. Cited incentive studies: Shanks et al. 2002; Vulkan 2000.
limits: The original paper (see a19) gives a looser threshold (under 10 with a symmetric utility). The three-times figure in the review is a summary and depends on the utility function.
agent_relevance: Cheap-sample regime: when one try costs little relative to the stakes of acting, draw one answer and go. Matches the schema's 'direct' mode.

source: Lieder & Griffiths (2020) Resource-rational analysis: understanding human cognition as the optimal use of limited computational resources (BBS 43:e1) - planning, strategy discovery, SAT-TTB
finding: Non-myopic resource-rational planning models (Callaway et al.) fit human planning operations better than prior heuristics. People reached about 86% of the best possible trade-off between decision quality and time cost, and matched the bounded-optimal strategy about 55% of the time. Aspiration levels fell as people gathered more information. An automatic derivation method (Lieder et al. 2017) found a new heuristic, SAT-TTB (satisficing plus take-the-best); a follow-up experiment found people use it where it is bounded-optimal.
numbers: 86% of the best quality/time trade-off; 55% agreement with the bounded-optimal strategy; SAT-TTB tested in the Mouselab risky-choice paradigm.
limits: Second-hand summary of Callaway et al. (published 2022 in Nat Hum Behav); I did not open that paper. Tasks are small, fully known lab problems.
agent_relevance: A quantitative benchmark: even a good human thinker is only about 86% of the best allocation of thought. A gate that gets within 80-90% of an oracle is a realistic target.

source: Lieder & Griffiths (2020) Resource-rational analysis: understanding human cognition as the optimal use of limited computational resources (BBS 43:e1) - frame problem and ignoring variables
finding: It is often resource-rational to ignore all but the one to three most relevant variables (Icard & Goodman 2015). This explains why people neglect alternative causes more in predictive than in diagnostic reasoning. Gabaix's sparse-attention model predicts base-rate neglect, sample-size insensitivity, overconfidence, projection bias and regression misconceptions.
numbers: Best number of variables to keep: 1 to 3 (Icard & Goodman).
limits: Review of other people's models; the work is theory plus fits to known biases, not new tests.
agent_relevance: Supports S1/S2 input trimming: keep the few variables that matter for the check, drop the rest.

source: Lieder & Griffiths (2020) Resource-rational analysis: understanding human cognition as the optimal use of limited computational resources (BBS 43:e1) - how much to think, anchoring
finding: Anchoring, which earlier work read as 'people think too little', fits an optimal speed-accuracy trade-off in the number of adjustments from an initial guess (Lieder et al. 2018). The proposed mechanism proposes small changes and accepts or rejects them probabilistically so the chain converges to the Bayes answer; later work links it to hypothesis generation and memory reuse (Dasgupta et al. 2017, 2018).
numbers: No new numbers in the review; see a17 for the model fits.
limits: A reinterpretation that fits published data; the review does not claim it rules out other accounts.
agent_relevance: Frames 'stopping early' as sometimes correct. Counters a blanket rule that more thinking is always better (G11, G12).

source: Lieder & Griffiths (2020) Resource-rational analysis: understanding human cognition as the optimal use of limited computational resources (BBS 43:e1) - challenges and boundary conditions
finding: Lists limits: needs enough adaptive pressure and experience; hard to apply when the environment or the constraints are unknown; costs are usually fitted, not measured; so models are hard to falsify. Irrational beliefs far from costly decisions are not evidence against it. Only simple, fully known lab tasks have been modelled so far; scaling to real decisions is open.
numbers: None numeric. Example: a memory strategy tuned for a span of 7 may be bad for a person with a span of 4.
limits: Authors' own list. Critiques sit in the commentaries (quantum cognition, enactivism and others), which I did not read.
agent_relevance: The main warning for us: the cost side is the weak point. If we cannot measure token cost and error cost, the rule is as good as our estimates.

source: Lieder & Griffiths (2020) Resource-rational analysis: understanding human cognition as the optimal use of limited computational resources (BBS 43:e1) - relation to Stigler and Gabaix-Laibson
finding: Differs from Stigler's information economics in two ways: Eq. 3 is a problem for evolution and learning, and it charges for the cost of thinking, not only the cost of collecting data. Gabaix and Laibson (2005) proposed a myopic rule: pick each cognitive operation by its immediate expected gain minus its cost. Gabaix et al. (2006) found this predicted people's suboptimal information search in a bandit task and fit multi-attribute choice better than earlier models.
numbers: No sample sizes given in the review.
limits: Myopic rules fail when value only appears after several operations; the review notes the benefit of one operation depends on the ones that follow.
agent_relevance: A myopic 'value of one more attempt' gate is cheap but can stop too early when gains arrive only after several steps.

source: Russell & Subramanian (1995) Provably bounded-optimal agents (JAIR 2:575-609)
finding: Separates four goals for an agent: perfect rationality (act to maximise expected utility, impossible since thinking takes time), calculative rationality (eventually returns what was rational at the start), metalevel rationality, and bounded optimality (the best program the machine can run in the environment). Defines bounded optimality for a program on a machine over an environment class, and shows it can be proved for some architectures.
numbers: Definition-level paper; includes asymptotic bounded optimality (worst-case and average-case, Definitions 13 and 14).
limits: Theory for agent programs; the proofs are for restricted architectures and task environments.
agent_relevance: The cleanest statement of what we want: not the best answer, but the best program under a compute budget. Fits G7 'the schema must pay for itself'.

source: Lewis, Howes & Singh (2014) Computational rationality: linking mechanism and behavior through bounded utility maximization (Top Cogn Sci 6:279-311)
finding: Applies bounded optimality to cognitive modelling: the theorist fixes a processor with its limits, fixes the environment and the utility, then finds the optimal policy on that processor and compares it to behaviour. Unlike classic rational analysis, it selects an optimal program, so it makes contact with mechanism.
numbers: Re-reported fit: a serial bounded machine predicted second-task response duration with mean R2 of 89%, 84%, 77% and 85% across four dual-task experiments (Howes et al. 2009).
limits: Architecture-first (fixed mechanism), where Lieder & Griffiths go function-first; the two share the bounded-optimality core. The R2 figures are from earlier work, quoted in this paper.
agent_relevance: Shows that a bounded-optimal policy can reproduce timing data; relevant if we wish to model our own agent's latency and token costs as the processor.

source: Gershman, Horvitz & Tenenbaum (2015) Computational rationality: a converging paradigm for intelligence in brains, minds, and machines (Science 349:273-278)
finding: Argues AI, cognitive science and neuroscience converge on intelligence as maximising expected utility net of the cost of computation. Metalevel reasoning chooses the algorithm and the stopping time t* from the expected value and cost of computation. Cites a study where people chose list-sorting strategies in a time-accuracy way, and a model where overestimating stressful rare events follows from utility-weighted sampling of a few hypotheses.
numbers: Figure 2 shows net value of action against stopping time t*. No new experimental numbers; the sorting result is Lieder et al. 2014 (a14).
limits: A review and position paper. The argument that the brain has metareasoning machinery is stated as an assertion needing evidence, per the text.
agent_relevance: Frames the stop/continue choice as value of computation versus cost of delay: the form our S0 and S4 gates need.

source: Lieder, Plunkett, Hamrick, Russell, Hay & Griffiths (2014) Algorithm selection by rational metareasoning as a model of human strategy selection (NIPS 27)
finding: Picks the algorithm a with the highest value of computation: VOC(a;i) = E[score] - E[opportunity cost of runtime]. Learned from a few features of the input by model-based learning. On sorting-algorithm selection it chose the best algorithm more often than two published machine-learning selectors.
numbers: Share of correct algorithm choices, ours vs Guo's decision tree: 99.78% vs 98.5%; 99.99% vs 99.4%; 83.37% vs 77.0%; 99.99% vs 85.3% on four test sets (nearly sorted, inversely sorted, random, and the combined set); all p < 1e-15.
limits: Sorting only; the authors call it a lower bound for harder problems such as planning and search, which were not tested. The column labels in the table are partly garbled in my text extraction.
agent_relevance: A working example of a learned per-input gate that beat hand-built selectors. Features of the input predicted which procedure to run, as an S0 classifier would.

source: Lieder et al. (2014) NIPS 27 - behavioural experiment on strategy choice
finding: 100 Mechanical Turk workers were trained on cocktail sort and merge sort (11 training trials), then chose a strategy for 18 test lists. People picked merge sort mainly when it was the faster strategy. Nine models from three older theories (RELACS, SSL, SCADS) failed to predict this; rational metareasoning predicted the pattern. People were even more adaptive than the model.
numbers: N=100. 83% of participants chose merge sort more often when it was superior (95% CI 74.9% to 89.4%; p<1e-11). Merge sort picked on 81.67% of long, nearly inversely sorted lists but only 29.83% (long) and 27.00% (short) of nearly sorted lists. Rational metareasoning p<1e-5 for the pattern; the other models p>=0.46. People beat the model, p<=0.02. Task time 24.7 +/- 6.7 min.
limits: One online study, one pair of strategies, short training. The models were given the same information as the people and their choices were simulated; no replication I found.
agent_relevance: Evidence that people pick procedures by input features and cost, not by past average success. Supports using problem features (S0) to choose a mode.

source: Lieder & Griffiths (2015) When to use which heuristic: a rational solution to the strategy selection problem (CogSci proceedings)
finding: People learn a model of how well each heuristic does on problems with given features, and pick by expected quality minus cost. In a new Mechanical Turk study with heterogeneous loan decisions (30 binary choices, six criteria) people were above chance, as feature-based selection predicted. Time pressure and probability dispersion raised the use of take-the-best and elimination-by-aspects in simulations of Payne et al. data, as people showed. Older theories (SSL, RELACS) handle uniform environments but not mixed ones.
numbers: N=120 Mechanical Turk workers; 64.6% correct choices (99% CI 62.5% to 66.6%; p<1e-15 vs chance). Performed worse on non-compensatory than compensatory trials, consistent with Rieskamp & Otto (2006) Experiment 1 (7 blocks x 24 trials), which the model also reproduced.
limits: Only 30 trials, with complex, noisy feedback, so learning was weak; the authors say this needs a longer test. Conference paper; the full test is in the 2017 Psychological Review paper.
agent_relevance: Heterogeneous environments are exactly our case (many problem types). A gate must key on features, not only on one running average.

source: Lieder & Griffiths (2017) Strategy selection as rational metareasoning (Psychological Review 124:762-794)
finding: Full version of the strategy-selection theory. Per the abstract (seen only in a search listing): people learn a predictive model of each strategy's performance and choose by best cost-benefit; systematic model comparisons supported it, and 4 new experiments confirmed distinctive predictions; people gradually learn to make more rational use of fallible heuristics.
numbers: 4 new experiments (sample sizes not read).
limits: Not opened this session; numbers must be checked in the paper before use. Page numbers differ between sources.
agent_relevance: The source to read next for the learning-to-gate claim.

source: Lieder, Griffiths, Huys & Goodman (2018) The anchoring bias reflects rational use of cognitive resources (Psychon Bull Rev 25:322-349; read as the author preprint)
finding: A model where estimates move from an anchor by repeated small accept/reject steps (a sampler) explains ten anchoring effects. Best number of steps trades time cost against error cost, so bias shrinks as the cost of error rises and grows as time gets costly. Fits two free parameters (step size and relative time cost) per data set.
numbers: Provided anchors (Jacowitz & Kahneman 1995): average anchoring index about 50%; fitted 29 adjustments, step 22.4 units. Self-generated anchors (Epley & Gilovich 2006): fitted 8 adjustments, step 10.06; model adjusted 80.62% of the distance vs 80.95% observed; insufficient adjustment on 13 of 19 questions, as in the data.
limits: Fits are to previously published results, with two free parameters each, so they show consistency, not a test. The paper says whether anchors are chosen rationally is 'still an open question'. A companion paper ran the prospective test (adjustment up with error cost, down with time cost).
agent_relevance: Direct case of 'stop early on purpose': the bias is the price of a short chain. Use caution before copying the model: the evidence is post-hoc fitting.

source: Lieder et al. (2018) - what the anchoring paper does and does not show
finding: The model reproduces effects of time pressure, load and alcohol (smaller adjustments), accuracy incentives and forewarnings, anchor extremity, and the finding that incentives help with self-generated but not provided anchors (Epley & Gilovich 2005). The incentive difference is explained by differing uncertainty, not by two processes. The authors call it 'a unifying, parsimonious, and principled explanation'.
numbers: Ten phenomena simulated (Table 1). Estimated adjustment counts differ a lot across data sets (8 vs 29), which the authors tie to scale of the quantities.
limits: No fresh data in this paper; the step size is a free parameter that absorbs scale. The choice of anchor is left unmodelled. The 'unifying' claim rests on qualitative agreement.
agent_relevance: The pattern 'bias falls as error cost rises' maps to: raise the thinking budget when the cost of being wrong is high.

source: Vul, Goodman, Griffiths & Tenenbaum (2014) One and done? Optimal decisions from very few samples (Cognitive Science 38:599-637)
finding: A sample-based agent that takes k samples per decision maximises reward per unit time with very small k when each sample costs time. Making many quick guesses from one sample can be globally optimal. This also gives a bounded-optimal account of probability matching, Hick's law and the variability of single responses.
numbers: Optimal k = 1 for action-to-sample time ratios under 10 with a symmetric utility; with no penalty for errors the ratio must be 2 or more before any sample is worth it. Re-analysis of 25 probability-matching studies (Vulkan 2000): stakes vs effective samples r(25)=.61, p=.0013, 95% CI .28 to .81.
quote: making many locally suboptimal decisions quickly is the globally optimal strategy
limits: The correlation is across studies that differ in many ways. The model assumes a fixed number of samples; sequential policies (SPRT) are also analysed and give similar small numbers. Assumes sample cost is known and constant.
agent_relevance: When action is cheap relative to a try, one sample can be right. But our setting differs: an extra LLM sample is not free and errors can be costly, so the ratio must be measured.

source: Lieder, Shenhav, Musslick & Griffiths (2018) Rational metareasoning and the plasticity of cognitive control (PLoS Comput Biol 14:e1006043)
finding: The Learned Value of Control (LVOC) model: people use reinforcement learning to predict the value of control signals (type and intensity) from stimulus features, with a cost for effort and time. It predicts the learning seen in one visual-attention experiment and four Stroop/Flanker experiments, and beats Win-Stay Lose-Shift and Rescorla-Wagner models.
numbers: 5 experiments re-modelled (Lin 2016 visual search; Krebs; Braem; Bugg Stroop/Flanker). The Lin learning curve was predicted with no free parameters; the Rescorla-Wagner fit used a learning rate of 0.0927 and under-predicted improvement. Win-Stay Lose-Shift did not capture gradual improvement.
limits: Simulations on published data, with auxiliary cost assumptions; the authors list only qualitative agreement for several effects. Cognitive-control tasks are short lab tasks.
agent_relevance: Learning when to apply effort from cues is the 'learned gate' idea. It argues for trial-and-error learning of the gate's thresholds from our own run logs.

source: Callaway, Rangel & Griffiths (2021) Fixation patterns in simple choice reflect optimal information sampling (PLoS Comput Biol 17:e1008863)
finding: Treats gaze in food choice as information sampling and approximates the optimal policy. It is best to sample options whose value estimates are both high and uncertain. The model accounts for fixations and choices in binary and trinary choice, and for the gaze-choice link, as well as the standard attentional drift-diffusion model (aDDM) does or better on some measures.
numbers: Two datasets: binary and trinary food choice; each participant rated 70 snacks (-10 to 10) and made 100 choices among positively rated items, eye position at 50 Hz.
limits: Mixed: the aDDM is better on some fixation patterns, but the authors note it samples durations from the observed data, so its fit is partly built in. Models with some prior bias fit the binary fixation curves better than an unbiased version.
agent_relevance: Value-of-information search where to look next: the same logic as 'which part of the problem is worth a second look'.

source: Callaway, Gul, Krueger, Griffiths & Lieder (2018) Learning to select computations (UAI 2018; arXiv 1711.06892)
finding: Bayesian metalevel policy search (BMPS) learns a policy for choosing computations by treating the value of a computation as lying between the myopic value of information and the value of perfect information. It was near-optimal on three metareasoning problems: when to stop, how to allocate computation across options, and planning.
numbers: Tree domain: 99.1% of optimal return (0.6535 vs 0.6596, t(1998)=-7.43), vs meta-greedy 0.60, full deliberation 0.20, DQN 0.58 (all p<1e-15). Planning domain (depth 2 and 3 trees): 98.4% of optimal (0.367 vs 0.373). A tornado-evacuation case shows gains survive the metareasoning overhead.
limits: Small, fully specified toy problems where the optimal policy can be computed; two-column text extraction made the mapping of results to sub-domains uncertain. Not tested on language tasks.
agent_relevance: Gives a concrete, learnable approximation to the gate: a few features of the current belief state predict the value of one more computation. Full deliberation (0.20) scored far below a good gate.

source: Correa, Ho, Callaway & Griffiths (2020) Resource-rational task decomposition to minimize planning costs (CogSci; arXiv 2007.13862)
finding: Task decomposition (choosing subgoals) is modelled as a resource-rational representation problem: pick the breakdown that most reduces planning cost for the planner in use. The model reproduces four experiments from Solway et al. (2014), including bottleneck states being chosen as subgoals; with breadth-first search in a graph where subgoals do not help, it learns to use none.
numbers: Replicates the qualitative results of Solway et al. (2014) Experiments 1 to 4 (graph navigation); no new sample sizes.
limits: Qualitative replication by simulation; depends on the planner assumed. Small graphs.
agent_relevance: Gives a rule for when decomposition pays: only when it lowers search cost. Matches 'search only with a foothold' (G12).

source: Godara & Aleman (2024-2026) A resource rational account of the explore-exploit dilemma via metareasoning (meta-BAMDP; arXiv 2408.01253)
finding: Extends metareasoning to bandits with unknown rewards (a meta Bayes-adaptive MDP) and proves two theorems that make it tractable. As the cost of computation c rises, the value of planning falls; the model reproduces human adaptation to cognitive load, suggests directed exploration is computationally costlier than exploitation, and offers an account of the IQ-bandit correlation.
numbers: Policies evaluated by 1e5 simulated agents per setting; Bernoulli bandits with varying arms N and horizon T.
limits: Theory and simulation with approximate solutions; the human comparisons are qualitative and rest on earlier data, with no new human experiment. The paper says experimental tests are still needed.
agent_relevance: Links metareasoning to exploration vs exploitation, which another subfield covers. The result 'higher cost c means less planning and a greedy terminal move' is a testable prior for our budget rule.

source: De Sabbata, Sumers, AlKhamissi, Bosselut & Griffiths (2024) Rational metareasoning for large language models (arXiv 2410.05563)
finding: Turns the value of computation into a training reward: R(x,y,z) = U(z|x,y) - lambda*length(z), where U is the log-probability gain on the target answer from the chain of thought z. Trained with expert iteration (rejection sampling, advantage = reward minus mean). Compared to few-shot CoT and STaR on Llama-3.2-3B and Llama-3.1-8B (base and instruct).
numbers: Averaged over datasets, one 8B model: accuracy 63.5% (RaM, 146.2 output tokens) vs 61.9% (STaR, 215.1 tokens) vs 56.4% (CoT few-shot, 253.6 tokens); another: 50.1% (170.8 tokens) vs 47.4% (222.7). Overall 23-45% fewer tokens across three models, with accuracy equal or higher. Out-of-distribution on MMLU-CF: 28-36% fewer tokens than STaR at similar accuracy.
limits: Needs ground-truth answers for the reward; trained small open models; the pairing of table rows and model names is jumbled in my text extraction, so rows should be checked against the PDF before quoting. The model was trained, which our no-training scaffold cannot copy.
agent_relevance: The one direct LLM test of a VOC rule: it cut tokens a lot while keeping accuracy. A prompt-time gate may capture part of the saving with no training; unknown.

source: De Sabbata et al. (2024) - adaptivity analysis
finding: Splitting items by whether a direct answer was correct (easy) or not (hard), all methods wrote shorter reasoning on easy items. RaM widened the gap most. Instruction-tuned CoT prompting did not adapt length to difficulty.
numbers: Mean reasoning tokens, hard vs easy: RaM 145 vs 72 (50.3% shorter on easy), 139 vs 89 (36.0%); STaR 195 vs 128 (34.4%) and 202 vs 129.5 (35.9%); CoT few-shot 210 vs 170 (19.0%) and 197.5 vs 151 (23.5%); CoT prompting 222 vs 221 (0.5%) and 228 vs 226 (0.9%).
limits: 'Easy' is defined by the same model's direct-answer success, a noisy difficulty label. Authors cite Sprague et al. (2024): CoT helps mainly on math and logic, with small gains elsewhere.
agent_relevance: Plain instruct models with CoT prompts spend about the same tokens on easy and hard items. A gate that routes by difficulty has room to save tokens.

source: Hu, Roshan & Varma (2026) Are more tokens rational? Inference-time scaling in language models as adaptive resource rationality (arXiv 2602.10329)
finding: Variable Attribution Task: models find which variables determine an outcome from trials and a logic function, with the number of candidate variables N and trials T varied. DeepSeek R1/V3 and Qwen3-80B Thinking/Instruct switched from a permutation (pairwise) strategy at small N (N<4) to an elimination strategy as N grew, with no cost term in training. Instruction-tuned models degraded on XOR and XNOR; reasoning models stayed robust. XOR/XNOR drew longer traces (higher intercept and steeper slope).
numbers: Strategy labels checked against a human-labelled set of 100 balanced examples. Logistic model fit for elimination use: AIC 2727.29 and pseudo-R2 0.160 for the best interaction model (logN, T), vs AIC 3178.55 and pseudo-R2 0.019 for T alone; terms p<0.001.
limits: Single synthetic task and two model families; pseudo-R2 values are low (0.16 at best). The authors give a rival reading: trace length may reflect limits of attention-based state keeping, not deliberate allocation. Strategy labels checked on only 100 examples. Qwen mostly avoided elimination on XOR.
agent_relevance: Suggests strategy shifts with problem size already occur in LLMs without any cost reward, which supports a lighter gate. The evidence is thin and there is a stated alternative.

source: Wang et al. (2026) R3-Bench: LLMs struggle with resource-rational reasoning under shared budgets (arXiv 2608.16033)
finding: Six-problem contests (maths, competitive programming, abstract reasoning; tool-free and agentic) share one budget. An offline 'oracle' built from the same model's single-problem response curves is compared with actual contest scores. Models fall short of what they can do alone; strategy updating is limited and failures depend on budget pressure.
numbers: 72 main-table cells for six models: oracle mean >= contest mean in all 72 and strictly higher in 71. Under moderate tool-free pressure an equal-allocation replay beats the actual contest score for three of six models. In a three-model strong-pressure agentic check, at least one fixed scheduler beat the contest mean in six of nine cells, but no policy won everywhere. 50 contests per domain.
limits: The oracle is offline and empirical (an upper bound, not a policy anyone can run live). Only some models and settings; no policy dominates across domains.
agent_relevance: Direct evidence that LLMs allocate a shared budget poorly. Code-based allocation (fixed schedules) can beat the model's own allocation, in line with 'the program decides, the model fills slots'.

source: Wang (2026) Humans disengage, reasoning models persist (arXiv 2606.26502)
finding: Separates difficulty registration (trace length follows human problem duration) from deliberation allocation (what happens on a problem once it is hard). Across H-ARC, INTUIT and Cortes, six open thinking LRMs and DeepSeek-V3 register difficulty like humans, but allocate differently: successful human attempts are longer than failed ones (once item is controlled), while failed LRM attempts are longer than successful ones. Failed LRM traces hold more hedging (H-ARC) and repetition (Cortes).
numbers: H-ARC humans: within-item correctness slope +0.24 log units; adding log(1+actions) cuts it to +0.125. Wrong H-ARC trials: fastest quartile median 16 grid edits, slowest 79. Each LRM has at least 298 H-ARC observations, except gpt-oss-20b (n=119).
limits: Observational, item-matched data; trace length is not the same as computation; Cortes shows a more mixed picture (successful attempts longer in separate analyses). Single-author preprint.
agent_relevance: Long traces on a failing problem are a failure sign in LRMs, not a sign of effort paying off. Supports a stop rule tied to progress, not to length (G1, G11).

source: Sprague et al. (2024) To CoT or not to CoT (meta-analysis, as cited by De Sabbata et al.)
finding: Cited in the RaM paper as a meta-analysis of over 100 papers finding that explicit chains of thought help mainly on maths and logic, with marginal gains elsewhere.
numbers: Over 100 papers (as reported by De Sabbata et al.).
limits: Second-hand: not opened this session. Use only as a pointer.
agent_relevance: Supports the idea that a gate should send non-math, non-logic items to direct or short reasoning.

source: Russell & Wefald (1991) Principles of metareasoning (Artificial Intelligence 49) and Horvitz (1987-89), as cited in the BMPS paper
finding: Rational metareasoning, introduced to give machines intelligent control over computation: choose computations whose expected value exceeds cost, stop when the expected benefit falls below the cost. The BMPS paper notes it is computationally intractable in general (Hay et al. 2012), which is why approximations are learned.
numbers: No numbers in the cited passage; the BMPS paper opens by contrasting Deep Blue's 200 million positions per second with Kasparov's about 3.
limits: Not opened; known only from the BMPS introduction. Original papers should be read for the formal VOC definitions.
agent_relevance: The root of our stop rule. The intractability is the reason to use a learned or table-based gate rather than exact VOC.
